In this exercise you will compare groups while keeping the raw data visible.

The aim is to avoid plots that show only summaries when the distribution and individual observations matter.

Main job: **compare different plotting choices and decide which one is most honest for the question**.

## Load packages and data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
blomkvist <- read_csv("data/blomkvist.csv")
blomkvist <- drop_na(blomkvist, smoker, rt_hand_d)
```

## Data structure for group comparisons

For group-comparison geoms, the grouping variable and the outcome variable need to be in the same data frame. Here, each row is one participant.

| Geom or layer | Data structure it needs | Typical mapping |
|---|---|---|
| `geom_jitter()` | one categorical grouping variable and one numeric outcome | `aes(x = group, y = outcome)` |
| `geom_boxplot()` | one categorical grouping variable and one numeric outcome | `aes(x = group, y = outcome)` |
| `stat_summary()` | one grouping variable and one numeric outcome to summarise | `aes(x = group, y = outcome)` |

<p class="take-home">For these plots, groups should usually be values in one column, not separate columns.</p>

## Start with raw points

Use jittered points to compare dominant-hand reaction time across smoking groups. This geom needs `smoker` as the grouping column and `rt_hand_d` as the numeric outcome column.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.45) +
  labs(x = "Smoking status",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

What does this show well? What is still difficult to compare?

## Add a summary without hiding the data

Add a boxplot on top of the jittered points. The boxplot uses the same data structure as the jittered points: group on `x`, numeric outcome on `y`. Hide the boxplot outliers because the raw points already show all observations.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = smoker, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.8) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = ___) +
  labs(x = "Smoking status",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

How does the boxplot change what is easy to compare?

## Why not a bar plot?

The plot below shows group means as bars. Run it, then compare it with the raw-data plot above.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = smoker, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", fill = "grey70") +
  labs(x = "Smoking status",
       y = "Mean dominant-hand reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

What does the bar plot hide?

## A better summary overlay

Instead of bars, add means and confidence intervals on top of the raw data. `stat_summary()` uses the same grouping and outcome columns, but calculates summary values before drawing.

```{r}
ggplot(data = blomkvist, mapping = aes(x = smoker, y = rt_hand_d)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, colour = "#D55E00") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal,
               geom = "errorbar",
               colour = "#D55E00",
               width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Smoking status",
       y = "Dominant-hand reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Does this plot communicate both the summary and the variation? Why?
